sentences: Two women dressed in white are walking across the sand by the sea.
The breeze pulls their skirts and thin veils backward, and behind them the blue water rises almost to the top of the picture.
This is Strolling along the Seashore, painted in the summer of 1909 by the Spanish artist Joaquín Sorolla.
The two women are his wife, Clotilde, and their eldest daughter, María.
The canvas is almost square, about two metres each way, and the figures are close to life-size.
Sorolla was born in Valencia in 1863.
He lost both parents at about the age of two and was raised by relatives.
In 1900 he won the Grand Prix at the World's Fair in Paris, and his name spread across Europe.
Early in 1909 he held his first American exhibition in New York, and it was a huge success.
That summer he went home to the beach at Valencia and painted almost without stopping.
This picture comes from that summer.
Now look at Clotilde, on the left.
She wears a wide straw hat, and with her right hand she holds down a thin veil that the wind keeps trying to lift away.
In her left hand she carries an open white parasol.
Notice that the top of her hat is cut off by the edge of the canvas.
Now look at María beside her.
Her face is open to the light, and she lets her own hat hang from one hand.
Both women wear white, but look closely.
That white is mixed with touches of blue, yellow and lilac.
Look down at their feet.
Long shadows stretch across the sand, because the sun is already low.
Along the bottom of the picture, a wide band of empty sand is left with nothing in it.
Now raise your eyes.
Sorolla looked down on the scene from a slightly higher point, so there is no horizon.
Instead, a single white line of foam runs across the top.
The water is painted in long strokes of blue, mauve and turquoise, which the museum calls an abstract backdrop.
The cut-off hat and the empty sand make it feel like a photograph of one passing moment.
On this beach Sorolla often painted fishermen at work and children in the waves.
This is different: an elegant stroll by well-dressed people beside the sea.
Sorolla kept this painting until his death in 1923.
Today it hangs in the Sorolla Museum in Madrid, his former home and studio.
Clotilde left the house and its contents to the state, and the museum opened in 1932.
Step back and take in the whole canvas.
Two people walk slowly through wind and sunlight.
Today, when the wind blows, stop for a moment and watch what it moves as it passes.
